verdict.reasoning: The gap — better methods for enforcing Lipschitz constraints in neural networks, improving upon weight clipping — has been addressed by multiple subsequent works. Gradient penalty (Paper 1) directly solves the problem for WGAN critics, replacing weight clipping with a principled gradient-norm penalty that yields more stable training and better capacity use. Adversarial Lipschitz Regularization (Paper 3) goes further, providing a general-purpose explicit Lipschitz penalty viable via adversarial perturbation search, demonstrated on GANs but not tied to the GAN framework. CoWGAN (Paper 4) offers yet another alternative using c-transform objectives, theoretically grounded and computationally efficient. While each method has some context specificity or hyperparameter tuning needs, together they constitute a clear affirmative answer: better methods do now exist and demonstrably outperform weight clipping. The remaining open aspects (e.g., perfecting adversarial perturbations, handling batch normalization) are refinements, not signs that the core gap remains unaddressed.

paper.title: Improved Training of Wasserstein GANs
paper.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are powerful generative models, but suffer from training instability. The recently proposed Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) makes progress toward stable training of GANs, but sometimes can still generate only low-quality samples or fail to converge. We find that these problems are often due to the use of weight clipping in WGAN to enforce a Lipschitz constraint on the critic, which can lead to undesired behavior. We propose an alternative to clipping weights: penalize the norm of gradient of the critic with respect to its input. Our proposed method performs better than standard WGAN and enables stable training of a wide variety of GAN architectures with almost no hyperparameter tuning, including 101-layer ResNets and language models over discrete data. We also achieve high quality generations on CIFAR-10 and LSUN bedrooms.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper directly addresses the gap of needing better Lipschitz constraint enforcement methods for neural networks, specifically in the context of Wasserstein GANs. The authors identify that weight clipping (the original method) leads to problems like capacity underuse and gradient exploding/vanishing, and propose gradient penalty (GP) as a superior alternative. They show that gradient penalty enforces the Lipschitz constraint more effectively, leads to more stable training, and enables the critic to learn richer function classes. The paper systematically compares gradient penalty to weight clipping and other variants, demonstrating clear improvements.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully solves the specific gap it addresses — better Lipschitz constraint enforcement for WGANs. However, the gap as stated is broader ("better methods needed for enforcing Lipschitz constraints in neural networks"). The paper focuses on one specific approach (gradient penalty) in one specific context (WGAN training with a critic network). It does not explore other possible Lipschitz enforcement methods (e.g., spectral normalization, which came later; orthogonal regularization; or Lipschitz-constrained architectures), nor does it address enforcing Lipschitz constraints in other neural network contexts beyond GANs. So while it is a direct and substantial solution to the gap as framed by the original WGAN paper, the broader gap of "better Lipschitz enforcement methods in neural networks" remains partially open for other architectures and applications.
evidence_snippets: We propose an alternative to clipping weights: penalizing the norm of gradient of the critic with respect to its input.
Weight clipping leads to undesired behavior ... we instead penalize the critic if its gradient norm moves away from its target norm value 1.
Our method converges faster and to better optima than weight clipping, and is far more robust to hyperparameter selection than other WGAN training methods.

paper.title: A Wasserstein GAN model with the total variational regularization
paper.abstract: It is well known that the generative adversarial nets (GANs) are remarkably difficult to train. The recently proposed Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) creates principled research directions towards addressing these issues. But we found in practice that gradient penalty WGANs (GP-WGANs) still suffer from training instability. In this paper, we combine a Total Variational (TV) regularizing term into the WGAN formulation instead of weight clipping or gradient penalty, which implies that the Lipschitz constraint is enforced on the critic network. Our proposed method is more stable at training than GP-WGANs and works well across varied GAN architectures. We also present a method to control the trade-off between image diversity and visual quality. It does not bring any computation burden.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper proposes Total Variational (TV) regularization — specifically the term |D(x) - D(˜x) - δ| — as an alternative to weight clipping and gradient penalty for enforcing the 1-Lipschitz constraint on the discriminator in Wasserstein GANs. The authors provide a rough proof that this TV term enforces an approximate Lipschitz constraint, and demonstrate empirically that their TV-WGAN is more stable during training than GP-WGAN, avoiding gradient explosion and loss fluctuation. The method is simpler (no gradient computation needed) and works across different network architectures.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper addresses the specific WGAN Lipschitz enforcement problem but only partially solves the broader gap of "better Lipschitz constraint enforcement." First, the proof of Lipschitz enforcement is rough and approximate (the authors derive a k-Lipschitz constraint where k = ε/η, not exactly 1-Lipschitz), and relies on questionable assumptions (e.g., that ∇_x D(x) > 0 and ∇_˜x D(˜x) < 0 always hold). Second, the method is specific to the WGAN setting where paired real/fake samples exist — it does not provide a general-purpose technique for enforcing Lipschitz constraints in arbitrary neural networks. Third, the approach only enforces a bound on the difference between outputs at two specific points (real vs. fake), not a global Lipschitz constraint across the entire input space. Fourth, the paper does not compare against other Lipschitz enforcement methods that emerged around the same time (e.g., spectral normalization, which was published shortly after). The gap of developing principled, general, and provably correct Lipschitz enforcement methods for neural networks remains largely open.
evidence_snippets: In this paper, we combine a Total Variational (TV) regularizing term into the WGAN formulation instead of weight clipping or gradient penalty, which implies that the Lipschitz constraint is enforced on the critic network.
The marginal TV regularizing term |D(x)-D(\widetilde{x})-\delta| in equation~[REF:e6] enforces the 1-Lipschitz constraint on the discriminative function D(x).
In this section, we prove that the 1-Lipschitz constraint is enforced approximately by the TV regularization.

paper.title: Adversarial Lipschitz Regularization
paper.abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are one of the most popular approaches when it comes to training generative models, among which variants of Wasserstein GANs are considered superior to the standard GAN formulation in terms of learning stability and sample quality. However, Wasserstein GANs require the critic to be 1-Lipschitz, which is often enforced implicitly by penalizing the norm of its gradient, or by globally restricting its Lipschitz constant via weight normalization techniques. Training with a regularization term penalizing the violation of the Lipschitz constraint explicitly, instead of through the norm of the gradient, was found to be practically infeasible in most situations. Inspired by Virtual Adversarial Training, we propose a method called Adversarial Lipschitz Regularization, and show that using an explicit Lipschitz penalty is indeed viable and leads to competitive performance when applied to Wasserstein GANs, highlighting an important connection between Lipschitz regularization and adversarial training.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes Adversarial Lipschitz Regularization (ALR), a method that enforces Lipschitz constraints by explicitly penalizing violations found via adversarial perturbation. Unlike prior explicit Lipschitz penalties that used random sample pairs (which were infeasible on complex datasets), ALR uses power iteration to find input perturbations that maximally violate the Lipschitz condition, making explicit Lipschitz regularization viable. The method is demonstrated on Wasserstein GAN critics (requiring 1-Lipschitz), achieving state-of-the-art Inception Score and FID on CIFAR-10 among non-progressive-growing methods, and competitive performance on CelebA-HQ with Progressive GANs.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the gap of needing better methods for enforcing Lipschitz constraints. It proposes a novel, effective method (ALR) that demonstrably works where prior explicit Lipschitz penalties failed. The paper itself identifies some remaining open aspects: (1) the approximation of the adversarial perturbation is imperfect and could be improved with other adversarial example generation methods; (2) the method introduces additional hyperparameters ($\lambda$, $P_\epsilon$, $\xi$, $k$) that require tuning; (3) the interaction between batch normalization and Lipschitz continuity is left for future work; (4) the method did not beat Gradient Penalty in the high-dimensional Progressive GAN setting on CelebA-HQ. However, these are refinements of the proposed solution, not an indication that the core gap remains unaddressed.

We hypothesize that using the explicit Lipschitz penalty in itself is insufficient because if one takes pairs of samples x, y randomly from P_r, P_g or P_i ... a more sophisticated strategy for sampling pairs is required. As we will show, a carefully chosen sampling strategy can in fact make the explicit penalty favorable over the implicit one.

Applying ALP on the critic in WGAN (WGAN-ALP), we show state-of-the-art performance in terms of Inception Score and Fr\'echet Inception Distance among non-progressive growing methods trained on CIFAR-10

paper.title: Training Wasserstein GANs without gradient penalties
paper.abstract: We propose a stable method to train Wasserstein generative adversarial networks. In order to enhance stability, we consider two objective functions using the $c$-transform based on Kantorovich duality which arises in the theory of optimal transport. We experimentally show that this algorithm can effectively enforce the Lipschitz constraint on the discriminator while other standard methods fail to do so. As a consequence, our method yields an accurate estimation for the optimal discriminator and also for the Wasserstein distance between the true distribution and the generated one. Our method requires no gradient penalties nor corresponding hyperparameter tuning and is computationally more efficient than other methods. At the same time, it yields competitive generators of synthetic images based on the MNIST, F-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 datasets.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes CoWGAN, a novel algorithm that enforces the 1-Lipschitz constraint on the discriminator in Wasserstein GANs without using weight clipping or gradient penalties. It uses multiple c-transform-based objective functions (J1, J2, J3, J4) and enforces the Lipschitz condition by comparing these objectives and optimizing the one that violates the admissibility condition. The method is theoretically motivated (Theorems 1 and 2 show the connection between objective function inequalities and the Lipschitz condition) and experimentally shown to enforce the Lipschitz constraint effectively while being computationally faster than gradient penalty methods.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the gap's specific problem of finding better methods to enforce Lipschitz constraints in the WGAN context. However, the method is specifically designed for the 1-Lipschitz constraint on the discriminator in WGANs and relies on the c-transform structure specific to optimal transport. It does not provide a general-purpose technique for enforcing arbitrary Lipschitz constraints on arbitrary neural network architectures outside the WGAN/optimal transport setting.
evidence_snippets: We propose a fast and stable WGAN training algorithm that enforces a 1-Lipschitz bound without the need of introducing a gradient penalty. Consequently, no hyperparameter tuning for such a penalty is needed.
Our method implements the constraint without the need to explicitly penalize the gradients.
In Section~[REF:sec:estimatingW] we will experimentally show that even with a very small mini-batch size $n$, our algorithm can enforce the condition~[REF:eqn:con] effectively.

paper.title: Orthogonal Wasserstein GANs
paper.abstract: Wasserstein-GANs have been introduced to address the deficiencies of generative adversarial networks (GANs) regarding the problems of vanishing gradients and mode collapse during the training, leading to improved convergence behaviour and improved image quality. However, Wasserstein-GANs require the discriminator to be Lipschitz continuous. In current state-of-the-art Wasserstein-GANs this constraint is enforced via gradient norm regularization. In this paper, we demonstrate that this regularization does not encourage a broad distribution of spectral-values in the discriminator weights, hence resulting in less fidelity in the learned distribution. We therefore investigate the possibility of substituting this Lipschitz constraint with an orthogonality constraint on the weight matrices. We compare three different weight orthogonalization techniques with regards to their convergence properties, their ability to ensure the Lipschitz condition and the achieved quality of the learned distribution. In addition, we provide a comparison to Wasserstein-GANs trained with current state-of-the-art methods, where we demonstrate the potential of solely using orthogonality-based regularization. In this context, we propose an improved training procedure for Wasserstein-GANs which utilizes orthogonalization to further increase its generalization capability. Finally, we provide a novel metric to evaluate the generalization capabilities of the discriminators of different Wasserstein-GANs.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper investigates replacing gradient-norm regularization (used to enforce Lipschitz constraints in WGANs) with orthogonality constraints on weight matrices. It compares three orthogonalization methods (soft regularization, Cayley transformations, and iterative Björck orthogonalization), finding that iterative orthogonalization enforces the Lipschitz condition most effectively. The paper proposes a hybrid training procedure that uses iterative orthogonalization early in training and switches to one-sided gradient penalty later, achieving improved generalization and FID scores. It also introduces a new metric for evaluating WGAN discriminator generalization.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper addresses the specific problem of enforcing Lipschitz constraints in WGANs by substituting gradient penalty with orthogonality constraints. However, it does not fully solve the broader gap of "better Lipschitz constraint enforcement" because: (1) The proposed method still relies on gradient penalty in later training stages — it does not provide a purely orthogonalization-based solution that matches or exceeds state-of-the-art throughout training. (2) The paper focuses specifically on the WGAN setting (Wasserstein distance) rather than Lipschitz-constrained networks more generally. (3) The orthogonality constraint is applied to the discriminator only, not to general neural networks requiring Lipschitz constraints. (4) The method introduces a scheduling mechanism (switching from orthogonal to gradient penalty) that adds complexity rather than providing a simple, universally applicable Lipschitz enforcement technique. The gap called for methods that improve upon weight clipping broadly; this paper provides a partial solution specific to WGANs with a hybrid approach.
evidence_snippets: In this paper, we direct our attention on increasing the fidelity of learned distribution by investigating the possibility of substituting the Lipschitz constraint required by Wasserstein-GANs with an orthogonality constraint on the weight matrices during training.

We found the training with hard constraint orthogonalization methods to be stable and that all considered orthogonalization methods are able to enforce the Lipschitz constraint. However, the learned distributions did not exhibit the same fidelity as the distributions learned by established training methods.

In our proposed method, we use the advantages provided by orthogonalization during the beginning of the models training. ... We relax this condition for the later training phase and ensure the Lipschitz condition using the one-sided gradient normalization introduced in [CITE:petzka2018on].
